articles.title: Home Assistant’s iPhone app explains which connection it uses
articles.dek: A new guide checks the device’s permissions and shows whether the app is using the home address or its external route.
body: Home Assistant’s iOS app adds a guide for understanding how it connects at home and away. Opened from the server’s connection settings or internal-address screen, it explains the internal and external addresses, shows which is in use and checks which requirements the device already meets.

The guide distinguishes an open app from one running in the background and explains how the connection security setting affects the choice. It also corrects the location-permission explanation: Precise Location is needed to read the Wi-Fi network name while the app is open, with Always access additionally needed in the background.
Bruno Pantaleão Gonçalves contributes the screen, making the app’s existing connection rules visible without changing how it chooses an address.

pullRequests.title: Explain when the internal and external URL are used

articles.title: Home Assistant sends Roborock Q10 vacuums to a chosen spot
articles.dek: Position reporting and zone cleaning join a go-to action that pauses the vacuum near the requested destination.
body: Roborock Q10 owners gain Home Assistant actions to read the vacuum’s position, clean a selected zone and send it toward a chosen spot. The integration extends its existing Roborock controls to the Q10/B01 device family.

The go-to action has an unusual limit: Q10 firmware has no dedicated command for it. The supporting library starts the device’s smallest cleaning zone, 40 by 40 centimetres, and pauses the vacuum within 20 centimetres of the destination. It stops intervening if another task replaces that job.
Hmmbob tested the work on a Q10 running firmware 03.11.24: it stopped 13.2 centimetres from the requested point and stayed there. That measurement describes the reported test on one device.

articles.title: ESPHome takes control of devices whose firmware spans several files
articles.dek: Device Builder keeps a maker’s supporting files together instead of failing partway through importing the configuration.
body: Taking control of an ESPHome device can fail when its maker spreads the firmware configuration across several files. Device Builder imports those files as a package when a single-file import cannot preserve them, and ESPHome finds supporting assets beside the configuration that names them.

J. Nick Koston verified the changes with the NeatoFx speaker: its configuration could fail during import or report a missing custom interface file even though that file existed in the maker’s repository. The package import preserves the links between those files.

Files in the user’s own configuration folder still take precedence when both locations contain a match. The change supports configurations that include other files without requiring the maker to flatten them into one.

articles.title: Music Assistant controls shuffle for music started in Sonos
articles.dek: Shuffle and repeat follow the speaker’s active service, including sessions started outside Music Assistant.
body: Music Assistant gains shuffle and repeat controls for services playing directly on Sonos speakers. A session started in the Sonos app—such as Qobuz, YouTube Music, Apple Music or Amazon Music—can expose its supported controls and current play modes in Music Assistant instead of producing a “nothing playing” error.

Marcel van der Veldt extends the earlier support for recognized sources such as Spotify Connect. The speaker supplies the active service’s capabilities, and its temporary entry disappears when playback switches elsewhere or the paused session ends. This controls an existing Sonos session; it does not add the service to Music Assistant’s music library.

articles.title: Music Assistant stops Squeezelite playing static instead of music
articles.dek: A stream-start correction protects 24-bit WAV playback, with a companion fix for rapid track changes.
body: Squeezelite players connected to Music Assistant could burst into loud static instead of music when receiving 24-bit WAV audio. The correction makes the player wait for its audio format before reading the stream, avoiding discarded bytes that turn samples into noise.

The failure could affect WAV output and low-latency live sources such as Spotify Connect. Marcel van der Veldt also corrects a related startup failure during quick track changes: a delayed report from the previous stream no longer prevents the next one from playing.

articles.title: Home Assistant limits access to script contents to administrators
articles.dek: A permission check closes a route that exposed raw script configuration to any signed-in user.
body: Home Assistant closes a route that let any signed-in user retrieve a script’s raw configuration, including credentials written into its sequence. Access through that connection command requires an administrator.

Franck Nijhof brings the route into line with the existing protection for automation configuration and the other script-configuration interface. The change restricts reading the script’s definition; it does not change permission to run it.

articles.title: Alexa temperature requests stop switching Nest out of cooling
articles.dek: Home Assistant preserves an active thermostat mode so the requested temperature can reach the device.
body: Asking Alexa to change the temperature on a Nest thermostat could switch it from cooling into a combined heating-and-cooling mode and cause the new temperature to be rejected. Home Assistant stops treating Alexa’s preliminary turn-on request as a reason to change a thermostat that is already active.
Allen Porter’s fix preserves the current mode before the temperature request arrives. Turning on a thermostat that is actually off keeps its existing behavior.

articles.title: Music Assistant opens more controls to keyboard users
articles.dek: Playlist sharing, smart-playlist rules and other header actions gain focus and screen-reader labels.
body: Keyboard users gain access to five Music Assistant controls that previously responded only to mouse clicks. Playlist sharing, smart-playlist rules, audio-analysis details and two genre-management actions become buttons that can be reached with Tab and activated from the keyboard.
The controls also receive labels for screen readers and a visible keyboard-focus indicator. Marcel van der Veldt applies the change across the item header, keeping the existing visual layout.
